newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Tesco calms Irish suppliers, distributors.
newsitem.headline: Tesco calms Irish suppliers, distributors.

text.p: Tesco chief executive Terry Leahy told worried Irish suppliers, distributors and staff on Friday they had nothing to fear from its 630 million pound takeover of the Irish business of Associated British Foods. "I want to reassure Irish suppliers," he told a Dublin news conference. "As far as the suppliers are concerned I have been a buyer all around the world and I can only say that the Irish agri and food business is world competitive."
He said Irish suppliers have nothing to fear "... they have everything they need to be successful and they have a 15 billion pound business to go for."
He was responding to concern that Irish suppliers, distributors and staff would be sidelined by the British company which has a long history of own-brand produce on its shelves.
Leahy said he placed his first order with Irish food company Kerry Group Plc 10 years ago and that order was now worth 60 million Irish pounds a year.

"If I can use Scotland as an example when we acquired the Wm Low chain of stores (in 1994), all Scottish suppliers were concerned. At that time Tesco's combined purchasing in Scotland was 280 million pounds," Leahy said.
Today Tesco purchases 400 million pounds from Scotland mainly from small suppliers, he said.
"They (suppliers) have thrived by doing business with us and they now supply throughout the UK and the rest of Europe."
Leahy also reassured the 8,300 employees in Ireland and the local distributors that Tesco's move was positive for them.

"You won't see any rationalisation. We haven't bought this business to shrink it. We bought it to grow it and we spend shareholders money on building stores and improving stores and this is what we intend to do here," he said.
Leahy said what Tesco had done in the UK was a good example of how the group worked.

"We have created 35,000 new jobs in the last five years. When Wm Low was acquired we had similar concerns about job losses but we have increased the workforce there from six to seven thousand." Leahy said.
He said he hoped the Irish business, which Tesco saw as a successful business, would continue to grow "... and customers have to be served."
In terms of distribution Leahy said Tesco have actually grown employment in this area "... and that has been the case in Scotland also."
He said Tesco's venture in Ireland was good for the economy as a whole and would provide spin-off employment in many different sectors including service areas and technology.
"Basically it is good news all around," Leahy said.

"Tesco will bring to the company in Ireland a resource far greater than we could have ever generated for ourselves," Power Supermarkets Group chairman and ABF executive Don Tidey said. He said this resource will accelerate the further development and growth of the Irish business and make it into a European player.

Tidey said there was an inevitability in what has happened because he had been considering for some time how to maximize the potential of the Irish business "... and we decided that could best be realised through an alliance to another food retailer who was committed to the development of the business in much the same way as it has carefully been done up to now."
